schools.summary: Gregory the Great frames the debate as a wrestling-match: opponent after opponent (Eliphaz, Bildad, Zophar) presents himself against Job yet deals his blows upon the air; the impertinent ever answer by the opposite, so Zophar begins with insult.
Gill takes Zophar for the youngest, speaking last, with less modesty and prudence and more fire and heat, the more irritated that Job had not receded under the others.
Henry laments the intemperate passions of wise men in dispute; Zophar misrepresents Job as idle, impertinent, a mocker and a liar, that it might seem justice to chastise him.

Clarke calls Zophar the most inveterate accuser, excelling in 'sour godliness' and 'too crooked to speak in measured verse'; Wesley marks the rising harshness from Eliphaz to Bildad to Zophar, who falls on Job without mercy.

Ellicott sketches Zophar as the man of worldly wisdom and common sense (against Eliphaz the poet and Bildad the traditionalist), the most offensive of the three, dragging the argument down to his own level.

outliers.note: Reads the three friends' assault as a wrestling-match in which each fresh opponent takes his turn against Job, yet none reaches the height of his well-fenced breast; their smiting words are lost in empty air.

schools.summary: Gill hears Zophar brand Job a babbler with words but no matter, citing Bar Tzemach's 'a man of a multitude of words' who deserves answer only to expose his emptiness.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'shall the torrent of words remain unanswered, and shall the prater be in the right?', gloss the speaker's name as 'the yellow one,' and fix the idiom (rob debarim, responsum non feret).

Clarke renders 'to multiply words profiteth nothing' and fastens on 'a man of lips' (ish sephathayim); Wesley turns the question back — sometimes the multitude of words should NOT be answered, silence being the best confutation of impertinence.
Henry catches the double edge — whether or not such talk be answered, it should be met only by reason and grace, never by pride and passion.

Gill distinguishes lies in common (wilful untruths) from doctrinal lies (errors concerning God), allowing men should not be silent as deaf and dumb, but grounding it all on whether the case was rightly named.

Clarke protests the charge is 'a very severe reproof, not justified by the occasion' — Job's solemn speech was sarcastic perhaps, but not nonsense; Wesley identifies the alleged lies (Job's innocency, God's ways) and mockery (the friends' counsels, ch. 6:14).
Henry judges Zophar has painted a sober sufferer as a shameless liar and mocker; Job 'spoke the words of truth and soberness,' and charity puts the best construction, not the worst.
Gill takes the verse as brought to support the charge of lying, resting on words Job had used earlier.

Clarke presses 'my doctrine' (likchi) as 'my assumptions' and charges Zophar with begging the question, since Job never claimed his life pure and himself clean; Wesley: Zophar perverts Job's words, who denied being a hypocrite, not being a sinner.
Ellicott weighs whether 'clean in thine eyes' is before God, men, or Job himself, preferring God (cf. ch. 10:15), so Zophar wishes God would credit Job with the penalty still due.
Henry: Job had said 'Thou knowest I am not wicked' (ch. 10:7) but also owned 'I have sinned' — to infer a claim of sinless perfection was an unfair insinuation.
Gill reads the wish as Zophar's despair of moving Job himself; only God can stop his mouth, convict his lies, and show him his folly in thinking himself pure.

Clarke recoils — 'how little feeling, humanity, and charity is there in this prayer'; Wesley: 'let God plead according to thy desire; he would soon put thee to silence,' with a warning against interesting God in our quarrels.
Henry turns it to irony: Zophar is sure God would 'open his lips against thee,' yet when God did speak he 'opened his lips for Job against his three friends' (ch. 42:7).

outliers.note: Bursts out against the prayer itself — that a friend at a sufferer's side should long for God to appear not to comfort but to condemn shows 'how little feeling, humanity, and charity' is in it.

schools.summary: Gill reads the 'secrets of wisdom' as the deep mysteries of God — Trinity, the two natures, resurrection — shown only as God reveals them.

Henry takes them as the arcana imperii, the state-secrets of heaven; what we know is nothing to what we cannot know, and the sentence that God exacts less than iniquity deserves is a hard mercy — thankful we are out of hell (Lam. 3:39; Ps. 103:10).

Ellicott judges 'double to that which is' 'conveys no sense, and is not a translation'; Keil and Delitzsch reject the common renderings of the neighbouring terms (cheqer not 'comprehension,' tachlith not 'perfection').

Clarke labours tushiyah (substance/essence, rendered a dozen ways — Coverdale, LXX, Good), taking Zophar to compare the revealed wisdom with the hidden; Wesley reads 'double' as 'manifold,' the secret wisdom infinitely greater than the revealed, so God sees innumerable sins in Job.

debates.question: How is 'the secrets of wisdom, that they are double to that which is' to be rendered?

sides.position: 'double' = manifold — the hidden wisdom infinitely beyond the revealed
the received translation conveys no sense / the common renderings of the terms are wrong

schools.summary: Gill draws the line: that God is may be found from nature, but what God is — his nature and perfections — is past finding out; the wiser heathen knew a God yet reared altars to the Unknown.
Henry makes God's incomprehensibility the ground of submission: we may apprehend but not comprehend him — 'the eye can see the ocean, but not see over it' (cf. Acts 17:27; Eccl. 3:11).

Clarke answers with a rush of attributes — self-existent, eternal, infinite, immense, incomprehensible; Wesley reads 'find out' as discovering all the depths of his wisdom and the reasons of his actions.
Ellicott fixes the literal 'canst thou attain to the searching out of God?' — the question whether the search can ever reach its end.

Keil and Delitzsch fix the subject as the divine wisdom (Chokma), its absoluteness measured by four dimensions as the love of God in Eph. 3:18; Ellicott renders plainly 'the heights of heaven... it is deeper than the grave.'
Gill allows the wisdom but offers the Vulgate's higher turn, 'he that is God is higher than the heavens' — heaven being but his throne, the heaven of heavens unable to contain him.
Clarke reads the four measures as instances of created immensity, crowning the thought with Milton — 'these are thy glorious works, Parent of good!'

debates.question: What is the 'it' that is high as heaven and deeper than hell?

sides.position: the divine wisdom (the Chokma of v.6)
God himself, higher than the heavens (the Vulgate)
the immensity of created things — heaven, sheol, earth, sea

themes: high as heaven, deep as hell

schools.summary: Gill notes length ascribed to the earth and breadth to the sea, but God's perfections admit no dimensions; hence he is omniscient, omnipresent, incomprehensible, and found in Christ alone.

Keil and Delitzsch carry the measureless wisdom forward as the ground of God's irresistible sovereignty — 'if he cut off... who can hinder him?' — God passing to and fro in nature and summoning the guilty as in an ancient public trial.

themes: longer than earth, broader than sea

schools.summary: Gill runs the senses of the first verb — cut off the power of the wicked, or 'change,' or 'pass through' in judgment — in each case none can hinder him.

Clarke hears it turned on Job — 'if he cut off, as he has done, thy children; if he shut up, as he has done, thyself by this sore disease'; Wesley glosses cut off, shut up, gather, and reads 'hinder' as 'contradict or charge him with injustice.'
Ellicott shows the verse woven from Job's own words (ch. 4:15; 9:11-12), preferring that Zophar throws Job's statements back rather than the forensic 'arrest, imprison, hold assize.'
Henry lifts it to its height — if he that made all from nothing reduce all to nothing, or shut up in the net of affliction (Ps. 66:11), who can arrest the sentence or oppose the execution?

debates.question: How are the three verbs 'cut off, shut up, gather together' to be taken?

sides.position: forensically — if he arrest, imprison, and hold assize
an allusion to Job's own words / God's providential undoing of a man and his house

schools.summary: Gill reads 'men of vanity' — all men, lighter than vanity — whom the Lord knows through and through, so it is no wonder he does with them as he pleases.

Clarke fixes 'men of falsehood,' God seeing both what is in man and what man does; Wesley keeps the sense of active judgment — God perceives wickedness veiled with religion and will observe it as a judge to punish.
Henry paints the all-seeing Judge who observes vain men and bad men alike — all wickedness naked and open before him — and will 'reckon for it, though for a time he seem to keep silence' (Hab. 1:13).
Ellicott renders the last clause 'though he regardeth it not' — God seems not to see the wickedness he in truth perceives; Keil and Delitzsch keep the stress on knowledge that issues in reckoning.

debates.question: What is the force of the closing clause about the wickedness God sees?

sides.position: 'will he not then consider it?' — God surely will requite the sin he sees
'though he regardeth it not' — God seems, for now, not to notice

themes: consider it, or seem not to see

schools.summary: Gill reads 'hollow' man void of good who 'would be wise,' i.e. be thought so, though he allows the sense that he 'may be made wise' by affliction, or the rendering 'bold, audacious.'

Henry gives the traditional reading fullest voice — man vain, foolish, wilful like the wild ass's colt (ch. 39:5), and proud, reaching after forbidden wisdom and losing the tree of life for the tree of knowledge.

Keil and Delitzsch reject Gesenius's privative 'void of understanding' as against the accents, reading the two words as correlative (empty vs. acquiring heart); Ellicott owns the line 'extremely difficult,' laying out three ways to construe it and noting the colt = Job.
Clarke multiplies renderings (Coverdale, Houbigant, Chaldee, Vulgate) and confesses no end to the conjectures; Wesley reads man void of wisdom yet pretending to it, the colt ignorant and untractable.

debates.question: What is the sense of this notoriously difficult proverb?

sides.position: vain/empty man WOULD be (thought) wise though born a wild ass's colt — a low estimate of man's untaught nature
the hollow man is instructed and the colt 'born a man' — discipline could humanise even a fool
privative — 'man is empty and void of understanding' (rejected on the accents)
holders: Gesenius (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

schools.summary: Gill reads it as counsel to pray aright — a prepared heart and hands stretched out (the gesture of religious worship) toward the God just described.

Wesley: prepare the heart 'to seek God, turning bold contentions into humble supplications'; Clarke bids Job use the powers God gave, citing Prov. 16:1 (man's the preparation, God's the answer), yet names the premise — 'Job must be a wicked man, else he had not been afflicted.'

Henry lays out the steps of return (as Eliphaz ch. 5:8, Bildad ch. 8:5): first the heart changed and established, then the hands stretched out to take hold on God and covenant with him (2 Chron. 30:8).
Gill marks that the lifted hand must be holy, not full of blood, and that it is 'in thine hand' not 'in thine heart' — sin acted out and gain ill gotten.

Henry sets out the two-fold reform: amend the conversation and restore ill-gotten gain (Zacchaeus, Luke 19:8), and reform the family, not suffering wickedness to dwell in the tents — 'the guilt of sin is not removed if the gain be not restored.'
Keil and Delitzsch set it as the hinge of the appeal: put away the evil, and the surmounted grief will leave no trace, 'like water that flows by.'
Clarke names the governing assumption — that there must be 'some iniquity in his hand, and some wickedness tolerated in his family.'

Gill reads the lifted face two ways — before men (a good conscience) and before God (holy boldness at the throne of grace) — the believer, though not spotless in himself, made fair in Christ's righteousness.
Wesley keeps the three notes distinct: to lift the face is cheerfulness and holy boldness, 'without spot' a clear conscience, 'stedfast' a strong assurance of God's favour.

Henry gathers it into 'the work of righteousness shall be peace' (Isa. 32:17) — holy confidence toward God (contrast ch. 9:34; 1 John 3:21) and holy composedness within, yet notes Zophar dangles it as bribe and threat.

themes: lift up thy face without spot

schools.summary: Gill reads former afflictions swallowed in later prosperity (Joseph naming Manasseh), and the converted soul forgetting its spiritual poverty save to magnify grace.

Clarke pictures the sufferings as mountain floods that sweep all away and are soon drunk up by the sandy plains; Wesley: remembered 'no more than men remember a land-flood,' which goes as suddenly as it comes.
Henry deepens it — forgotten as the mother forgets travailing pains for joy of the child, wounds healed without scar; 'where sin sits heavily, affliction sits lightly' (Isa. 33:24).
Gill takes 'thine age' as the remainder of Job's days, lit by a prosperity outshining the noon sun.
Clarke reads the rest of life unclouded, the sun rising more and more unto the perfect day, calling the image 'correct and elegant'; Wesley: light signifies prosperity, shining brighter and brighter.

Ellicott renders 'thou shalt soar on high... like the morning' with wings (Ps. 139:9; Mal. 4:2), but owns many take the disputed word as 'darkness'; Keil and Delitzsch adopt that — 'if it be dark, it shall become as morning.'
Henry, without pressing the philology, has Job's eclipsed light shine out again more brightly, the setting sun outshining the noon.

debates.question: Is the key word 'thou shalt shine forth' a verb of shining or a noun 'darkness'?

sides.position: a verb — 'thou shalt shine forth / soar on high like the morning'
a substantive 'darkness' — 'though there be darkness, thou shalt be as the morning'

schools.summary: Gill reads 'secure' as safe from every returning evil, and 'confident' — full assurance in God's love and promises for this life and the next.

Clarke takes 'dig about thee' of digging for water/wells (Isaac's, Gen. 26:15), now found in peace with none contending (cf. ch. 5:23); Wesley keeps digging but spreads it — fix tents, plough (ch. 1:14), or fence the dwelling.
Ellicott sets the digging aside: the word means 'thou shalt look around, or search about thee,' both 'dig' and 'blush' being inadmissible here.
Henry: those with good hope are safe, hope being an anchor (Heb. 6:19); to 'dig about thee' is to be as safe as an army in its entrenchments — 'the way of duty is the way of safety.'

debates.question: What does 'thou shalt dig about thee' mean?

sides.position: literally dig — for water/wells, or entrenchment, or to fix tents and plough
'thou shalt look around, or search about thee' — not dig at all

schools.summary: Gill pictures Job lying down on bed or by his flocks, none disturbing him — not thieves like the Chaldeans and Sabeans, nor lions and bears and wolves.
Keil and Delitzsch fix the idiom of 'make suit' as, more literally, 'many shall caress thy cheeks' — suppliants stroking the face of one newly risen to win his favour.

Henry expounds both promises — undisturbed sleep the reward of those who return to God as their rest, and the courting of many, Zophar shrewdly foreseeing that once the tide turned Job would again be the darling of his country.
Gill reads the failing eyes of grief and envy, or of a vain looking for good and deliverance that never come.

Clarke: the wicked look for rescue but 'escape perishes from them,' their hope 'an exhalation of breath,' given up with their ghost — and he judges Zophar's premises good but his application to Job 'totally erroneous'; Wesley reads eyes failing, hope perishing, a hope as desperate as life's at the point of death.
Ellicott corrects the last clause — 'omit the as of comparison,' the hope not merely like but being the breathing out of the soul — and marks the close of 'the first part of this mighty argument.'

debates.question: Is the hope 'as' the giving up of the ghost, or the very expiring itself?

sides.position: 'as' the giving up of the ghost — hope like a dying breath
omit the 'as' — the hope IS the breathing out of the soul

outliers.note: Judges Zophar's premises in general good and his conclusions legitimate, 'but his application of them to Job's case totally erroneous,' still assuming Job a wicked man whom affliction was unmasking; and notes Zophar's knowledge scarcely reached beyond the grave.
